# Lean tools

Use a tool when the project cause or the process walk calls for it. Record what you saw. Leave times and counts blank until you measure them. An illustration is not your data.

## Wastes

Walk the process and write what you see. The seven wastes to look for:

1. Transportation: material or product moved farther than the work requires.
2. Inventory: more material or jobs waiting than the next step needs.
3. Motion: people moving or reaching in a way that does not change the product.
4. Waiting: people or machines idle while something else finishes.
5. Overproduction: making more, or sooner, than the customer pulled.
6. Over-processing: work the customer does not need, or a tighter spec than the CTQ.
7. Defects: work that fails the spec and must be redone or scrapped.

Unused human skill is a common eighth. Add it when the team wants that category. It is an extension, not one of the original seven.

For each waste you record: place, what you saw, and your note. Do not mark a waste you did not see. Do not invent a count.

Blank row: place | waste type | what was seen | note

Illustration, not your data: place "pack cell", type "waiting", note "boxes sat 20 minutes while the label printer was down". Use this shape only. Use your own observation on the real sheet.

## 5S

5S is Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain, for one area.

1. Sort: what you removed, and where it went.
2. Set in order: where the remaining items live, so a stranger can find them.
3. Shine: what "clean" means here, and what you clean.
4. Standardize: the written standard for the first three steps.
5. Sustain: who checks, and how often.

Blank: area | removed | home for what remains | clean standard | who checks

Illustration, not your data: area "gage cabinet", removed "three expired stickers", home "hooks labeled by size", clean standard "no loose cards on the shelf", who checks "cell lead, Friday".

## Value stream map

Draw the current state, then a future state only after you have measured the current one.

For each step record: process time, wait time, and the information that triggers the step. Add material flow and information flow. Lead time is the sum of the times you entered. Process time is the sum of the process times you entered. If a time is missing, leave the total blank and name the missing step.

Do not draw a future state that assumes a time you have not measured. Mark a future-state time as a target when the user sets it, and keep it separate from the current-state time.

Blank step row: step name | process time | wait time | trigger | unit of time

Illustration, not your data: step "weld", process time "4 min", wait time "30 min", trigger "paper traveler". Lead time stays blank until every step in the real map has a time.

## Flow

Flow means work moves in one piece or in a small batch, and waiting is called waiting.

Write the batch size you use now, the batch size you will try, and where the work stops. A stop with no time stays a stop. Do not convert a stop into a savings number until the financial worksheet has a cost the user or finance supplied.

Blank: product | current batch | trial batch | where it waits

Illustration, not your data: product "bracket", current batch "50", trial batch "5", waits "before paint".

## Pull

A downstream signal authorizes the upstream step. The signal may be a kanban card or another signal you already use.

Write the signal, the maximum inventory that signal allows, and who acts when the signal is empty. If you do not have a maximum, leave it blank. Do not copy a maximum from a textbook.

Blank: upstream step | downstream step | signal | maximum inventory | who acts

Illustration, not your data: upstream "cut", downstream "weld", signal "red card", maximum "one tray", who acts "cutter".

## Kaizen

A kaizen here is a short cycle inside the project, not a substitute for the DMAIC tollgates.

Write: target condition, current condition, the countermeasures the team will try, the date, and the follow-up the owner accepted. Current condition uses facts you recorded. Target condition is a state you choose, labeled as a target.

Blank: target | current | countermeasures | date | follow-up owner

Illustration, not your data: target "changeover under 15 minutes", current "last three changeovers were 40, 35, and 38 minutes", countermeasure "stage the fixture before the line stops", date "the user supplies it", owner "the user names them".

## SMED

SMED (single-minute exchange of die) shortens setup. List every setup step. Mark each step internal (the process is stopped) or external (the process can keep running). The change to try is a step that can move from internal to external, or a step that can be shorter. Times stay blank until you measure them.

Blank: step | internal or external | time now | time after the change you will try

Illustration, not your data: step "fetch fixture", mark "internal today, external after staging", time now "blank until timed".

## Poka-yoke

Poka-yoke is a change that makes a mistake hard to make, or hard to pass on.

Write the mistake, the device or check, and how you will see that the mistake was stopped. A sensor or a fixture you have not tried stays a plan. Do not record a prevented defect count until you have counted it.

Blank: mistake | device or check | how you will see that it stopped the mistake

Illustration, not your data: mistake "bracket loaded backward", device "pin that blocks the backward seat", see it "the press will not cycle".
